newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Shenzhen seeks to rationalise power sector.
newsitem.headline: China's Shenzhen seeks to rationalise power sector.

text.p: Shenzhen, the booming Chinese Special Economic Zone over the border from Hong Kong, is seeking to shut most of its small-scale power plants once bigger, more environmentally-friendly plants come on stream by the end of the decade, Vice Mayor Li Decheng said on Tuesday.
"This will help lower electricity prices in the city and improve the investment environment of Shenzhen," Li told visiting reporters from Hong Kong.

Smaller plants, most of them built in the 1980s to meet rocketing demand as the once sleepy agricultural village developed into an industrial powerhouse, currently have a combined annual capacity of just 1,200 megawatts (MW).
"About 60 percent or 30 to 40 plants will be rationalised, which means they will be closed down when the larger plants start operating," the vice major said.
Some produce as little as 10-20 MW a year.
Electricity supplied by the new, larger power plants to the city's power grid costs about 0.5 yuan a kilowatt hour compared with 0.7 yuan a kwh from the smaller plants, he said.
Shenzhen planned to invest 160 billion yuan in increasing power generating capacity by a total of 4,200 MW by the year 2000.
The Qian Wan Power Station and the Shenzhen Eastern Power Station, the two largest projects in the works, are due to become operational in 1999 and 2001, respectively.
"Both plants will be built in cooperation with Hong Kong investors and that will benefit the whole (power) network in our district," Li said.

Hong Kong-based Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd, a unit of Hopewell Holdings Ltd, signed a letter of intent earlier on Tuesday to invest in Shenzhen Eastern, which will have a total capacity of 2,640 MW.
The Shenzhen municipality is also in the verge of signing a letter of intent with China Light & Power Co Ltd of Hong Kong and Japan's Kanematsu Corp to develop the Qian Wan plant.
The Shenzhen East plant was originally planned to be coal-fired facility but has switched to gas following a change in China's power policy towards cleaner production.
"Electricity generated by gas-fired power plants will probably be more expensive than that from coal-fired stations but the air will be cleaner," Li said.
Shenzhen was holding talks with foreign investors to build a Liquefied Natural Gas receiving plant with total storage capacity of 3 million tonnes, the Vice Mayor said.
"About 2.5 million tonnes of that will supply the Shenzhen Eastern plant while the remaining 500,000 tonnes will be for domestic usage by Shenzhen citizens," a Shenzhen official said.
China Light will be responsible for supplying natural gas to the Qian Wan plant.
An official of the Guangdong Electric Power Bureau said earlier that no more coal-fired power stations would be approved in the Pearl River Delta in order to safeguard the environment.
Coal-fired plants may be permitted in other parts of southern Guangdong province on a case by case basis but on a very limited scale, he added.
